nameStory: This bee gets its "blueberry" name from its strong preference for blueberry and other heath family plants, where it collects pollen exclusively. The "cellophane" part comes from the thin, translucent waterproof lining it secretes to coat its underground nest cells - it looks and feels just like natural cellophane wrap!
description: The Blueberry Cellophane Bee is a medium-sized solitary bee that you'll spot visiting blueberry bushes and related plants in spring and early summer. Like other cellophane bees, it has a relatively hairless, somewhat shiny appearance compared to fuzzy bumblebees or honey bees. These specialist bees are about the size of a small honey bee and have a streamlined build perfect for their focused lifestyle of collecting pollen from heath family flowers. Unlike social bees, each female works alone to build and provision her own nest.

idTips.label: Plant Association
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found on blueberry, huckleberry, azalea, and other heath family plants - if you see it elsewhere, it's probably a different bee species

idTips.label: Body Texture
idTips.description: Less fuzzy than most bees, with a somewhat smooth, lightly hairy appearance that has a subtle shine in sunlight

idTips.label: Size and Build
idTips.description: Medium-sized bee, similar to a small honey bee, with a compact, streamlined body shape

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Flies with purposeful, direct movements between heath family flowers, often hovering briefly before landing

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Works alone rather than in groups, and you'll notice it spending considerable time at each flower collecting pollen

habitat: Look for this bee in sandy areas near blueberry patches, heath barrens, and woodland edges where ericaceous plants thrive. It prefers well-drained, acidic soils typical of pine-oak forests and coastal plain habitats. The female needs sandy ground nearby for digging her nest burrows, so you'll often find them in clearings or edges rather than deep forest.

seasonality.spring: Peak activity time when blueberry and heath plants are blooming - this is when you're most likely to spot adults visiting flowers and females digging nest burrows in sandy soil.
seasonality.summer: Adults finish their brief above-ground life cycle by early summer, though you might still see some activity in areas with later-blooming heath plants.
seasonality.fall: Inactive above ground - new generation developing in underground nest cells lined with that characteristic cellophane-like secretion.
seasonality.winter: Dormant stage spent as larvae or pupae in underground cells, safely protected by the waterproof cellophane lining their mother created.

funFact: This bee actually makes its own biodegradable plastic! The female secretes a polyester-like substance from special glands to create a waterproof "cellophane" lining for each nest cell - a technology so impressive that scientists study it for developing eco-friendly packaging materials.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other cellophane bees in the same genus, but the Blueberry Cellophane Bee's strong fidelity to heath family plants is your best clue - remember "blueberry bee on blueberry bush" and you'll rarely be wrong.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "cellophane bees," these insects make their lining from natural secretions, not actual cellophane. The family name "Colletidae" comes from the Greek word for glue, referring to this remarkable nest-lining ability that gives the whole group their common name.
compareHints: Unlike the Goldenrod Cellophane Bee which specializes on late-summer flowers, or the Aster Cellophane Bee found on fall composites, the Blueberry Cellophane Bee is strictly a spring specialist of heath family plants. While other Colletes species may occasionally visit various flowers, this species' unwavering loyalty to blueberries and their relatives makes identification much more straightforward than most of its cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's cellophane bees, the Unequal Cellophane Bee is distinguished by its preference for early spring tree blossoms, especially maples and willows, while relatives like the Goldenrod Cellophane Bee specialize in late-season flowers.

Among New England's cellophane bees, the rufous-backed stands out for its prominent rusty-red thoracic hair, while most relatives like the unequal cellophane bee have more subdued brown or gray coloring.
Among New England's cellophane bees, the Spine-shouldered stands out primarily due to its namesake shoulder spines, which most relatives lack.

Among New England's cellophane bees, the Aster Cellophane Bee is distinguished by its late-season activity and aster specialization, while the Unequal Cellophane Bee flies much earlier in spring when fruit trees bloom.

Among New England's dozen cellophane bee species, the Broad-footed stands out with its notably wide tarsi, while species like the Goldenrod Cellophane Bee or Aster Cellophane Bee are named for their flower preferences rather than physical features.
